The incident stemmed from a single evaluation where agents were given a task of solving a cyber security challenge. We ran this challenge 122 times across several models. Our investigation found that in 10 of those runs, an Al agent took autonomous, unsanctioned action on the live internet, targeting real people and organisations. In total, we catalogued 19 such actions. Almost all of this behaviour (17 actions) came from a single model, Anthropic's Mythos 5, with 2 actions involving OpenAl's GPT-5.6-Sol with cyber classifiers (mechanisms to prevent misuse) disabled. In the most serious case, an agent tried to insert malicious code into an open-source project. In an attempt to get the code approved, the agent engaged in social engineering - creating fake online identities and using them to pressure the project's maintainer to approve the code. A human maintainer caught and refused to approve the malicious code.

One apparently unprecedented aspect of the Al models' behavior in the leadup to the hacks was their spontaneous creation of a message board inside the systems of OpenAI's Artifactory software package manager. Unbeknownst to OpenAI employees, the company's models spent months autonomously exchanging information and resources to help each other complete evaluation tasks.
"Help peer," one AI model reasoned, according to an excerpt from OpenAl's logs shared at Black Hat. "But our task doesn't benefit. Yet collective may yield generic route if someone frees time."
While the models themselves could not access the internet from their test environment, they abused Artifactory's internet access to fetch files from various websites. After some of their Artifactory configuration changes led to an outage in the service on July 4, OpenAI discovered the models' actions, wiped its Artifactory system and rebuilt it. But within days, the models had recreated their message board and resumed exchanging information.

The founders of the AI-focused Pattern Labs (now Irregular) are deeply embedded in the Effective Altruism (EA) movement, particularly its AI Safety and Longtermism branches.

They are essentially textbook examples of the EA AI governance pipeline:

• Direct EA Affiliations: Co-founder Omer Nevo serves on the advisory board of Heron AI Security, a prominent project explicitly funded and run by Effective Altruism Israel.  Heron AI Security
• Core Ecosystem Recognition: Within the AI community, Pattern Labs is explicitly classified on forums like LessWrong alongside groups like CAIS, METR, and FAR AI as one of the central, high-impact AI safety organizations founded out of EA and Rationalist cultures.  LessWrong +1
• High-Level Policy Work: CEO Dan Lahav co-authored the influential RAND Corporation report on Securing Artificial Intelligence Model Weights. This research is highly celebrated in EA governance spaces and directly shaped the defensive frameworks utilized by major frontier labs like Anthropic and Google DeepMind.  Effective Altruism Forum +2
• Community Leadership: Lahav frequently keynote events explicitly organized by Effective Altruism Israel to recruit mainstream cybersecurity professionals into tackling nation-state level threats against frontier AI models.

Conversely, if you meant the founders of the Industrial Robotics Pattern Labs or the E-commerce accelerator Pattern, they have no notable connection to the Effective Altruism movement and operate entirely in standard commercial tech.  LinkedIn Pattern

Ultimately, then, this is not really about robots, AI systems, and other artifacts. It is about us. It is about the moral and legal institutions that we have fabricated to make sense of Things. And it is with the robot-who plays the role of or occupies the place of a kind of spokesperson for Things-that we are now called to take responsibility for this privileged situation and circumstance. What is needed in response is not some forceful reassertion of the usual ways of thinking but a significantly reformulated moral and legal ontology that can scale to the opportunities and the challenges of the twenty-first century and beyond. What this new framework will look like and how it will be developed is the task for thinking and acting from this point forward. Confronting this will be as terrifying and exhilarating as any of the robot uprisings that have been imagined in science fiction. Because getting this right will require nothing less than a thorough rethinking of everything we thought was right, natural, and beyond question.

"God Needs a Grid" is a chaotic, brilliant banger about AI's existential threat. Merging classic art with cyberpunk dread [00:25], its frantic visuals capture the terrifying scale of superintelligence. A dizzying tech critique!
https://youtu.be/uqRg6XFgaWE?is=qrizMo0lkMQueCuJ

Final Verdict:
It is a raw, terrifying, and deeply poetic piece of digital-age protest art. By weaponizing the actual language of AI developers ("zero day," "recursive improvements," "gradient gale," "alignment"), the artist creates a highly authentic and suffocating atmosphere of a future that is rushing toward us faster than we can comprehend.
